item.title: OpenAI appoints Dali Rajic as Chief Revenue Officer
item.description:
OpenAI has appointed Dali Rajic as Chief Revenue Officer, where he will lead the company’s global revenue organisation.

Rajic joins OpenAI from cybersecurity company Wiz, where he most recently served as President and Chief Operating Officer. He was involved in building the company’s operations and customer-focused business before its acquisition by Google.

Before Wiz, Rajic served as President and Chief Operating Officer at Zscaler and as Chief Customer and Revenue Officer at AppDynamics.

Rajic will succeed Denise Dresser, who will leave OpenAI to pursue other opportunities following a transition period. Dresser will work with the business team during the transition to support customers.

The company credited Dresser with building its revenue team, strengthening relationships with major customers and developing its commercial operations as OpenAI expanded its enterprise business.

Rajic’s appointment comes as the company prepares for the next phase of growth in enterprise AI. His role will include developing the company’s revenue operations and scaling its sales organisation globally.

Commenting on the appointment, Greg Brockman, President and Co-Founder, OpenAI, “We’re moving into a compute-powered economy, with AI becoming embedded in every workflow. Denise has led our revenue organization through a formative period for the business and has worked tirelessly to get the team to where it is today. The way we’re deploying this technology is changing rapidly, and Dali will turn what we’ve learned into repeatable execution as we build out the full system to make AI broadly useful for people and businesses.”

Speaking on his appointment, Dali Rajic said, “OpenAI has extraordinary technology, products that more than one billion people already love, and enormous market pull. I’m excited to join the team, build on the momentum already in place, and lead the revenue organization as we help customers realize the full value of AI.”

item.title: Freedom in advertising today goes far beyond creative expression
item.description:
Every August, advertising borrows the language of independence. Flags appear in ad films, jingles turn patriotic, brands rush to say something about the nation. But ask people who actually work inside agencies what freedom means to them, and the answer has nothing to do with a campaign calendar. It is about who gets to speak in a meeting, who gets to fail without it costing them their job, and whether a twenty-four-year-old can tell a client the brief is wrong.

For Vinay Singh Sangwan, Co-founder of Verve Media, that distinction matters more than ever. "To me, freedom in advertising today goes far beyond creative expression; it's about creating an environment where people have the trust to question assumptions, contribute ideas regardless of hierarchy, and take ownership of outcomes," he says.

A similar view comes from Amitabh Sreedharan, EVP Growth, INNOCEAN India, who sees freedom as extending beyond the creative department itself. For him, it means having the room to challenge what a brief appears to be asking for, question the problem underneath it and bring perspectives that may not have been considered by the client. It also means being able to collaborate across traditional agency roles and take an idea into areas such as technology, culture, data or even new business models.

Advertising in India was political long before it was creative. The country's first advertising agency, B Dattaram & Co, opened in Bombay in 1905, the same year the Swadeshi movement began pushing Indians to boycott foreign goods and back domestic industry. Ads of that era were not selling lifestyle; they were selling identity, urging readers to choose Indian-made soap, cloth and oil as an act of resistance. Freedom, in that first chapter, meant using persuasion as a tool against a coloniser.

Independence changed the fight but not the tension. As Indian brands multiplied, so did the incentive to exaggerate. That is why the Advertising Standards Council of India was set up in 1985, formed by professionals from the advertising and media industry to keep Indian ads decent, fair and honest. It was a restriction the industry placed on itself, and a necessary one. False health claims, fake purity indicators, invented superiority over rivals, these checks did not shrink advertising's freedom so much as give it credibility.

Today the boundaries being tested are less about what an ad can claim and more about who gets a say in making it, and whether there will be a job left to make it in. Forrester now expects AI, automation and efficiency drives to cut the US advertising workforce by 15% by the end of next year, an estimate it has doubled from its original forecast. Closer to the ground, Indian agencies are said to be quietly letting go of around 10% of their staff every year just to protect margins, even as global names cut headcount. For example, Omnicom confirmed more than 4,000 layoffs following its merger with Interpublic, and Dentsu announced it would lay off 8% of its global staff after a dip in revenue.

Layered on this is a culture that was rarely gentle to begin with. Women make up close to 40% of the advertising workforce in India, yet the industry's bias against them tends to surface hardest the moment they become mothers, when career breaks and maternity leave quietly become reasons to withhold leadership roles. Against that backdrop, freedom becomes a demand for stability, for respect, for a say in decisions that affect a person's livelihood.

Rajni Daswani, Chief Growth Officer, People and Business at SoCheers, sees this shift as the defining one at the moment. "Can I question a brief without being seen as difficult? Can I disagree with a senior without worrying about the consequences?" she asks, adding that as AI lets anyone produce ten versions of an idea in minutes, "the real value of a person is not just producing more, but knowing which direction is worth pursuing."

For Himani Mangtani, Business Head at SW Network, Bombay, freedom similarly comes down to agency over one's choices, including how people think, what they say and how they choose to work. She argues that this requires trust and accountability rather than rigid rules around how a brief should be approached or how work should be done. "For me, that's what freedom at an agency looks like today: trust, ownership and the ability to make choices within the responsibility you have," she says.

The work that freedom once built

It is worth remembering what unshackled advertising once produced in India, because it explains why the industry still romanticises the word. Alyque Padamsee, who ran Lintas through the 1970s and 80s, built his most famous work on a simple observation. His research found that the average Indian housewife's only private time was the ten minutes she got to herself in the shower each day, a moment of imagined escape from a life of responsibility. Out of that insight came the Liril girl, dancing under a waterfall in 1985, an image that had nothing to do with soap and everything to do with a woman claiming a few unwatched minutes for herself. It became one of the most recognised campaigns in the country's history, precisely because Padamsee had the room to chase an insight.

Piyush Pandey built a different kind of freedom, rooted in language rather than imagery, giving Indian advertising a voice beyond a global template. Work like Fevicol's ads or Cadbury's ‘Kuch Khaas Hai’ endured because agencies were allowed to trust an instinct.

None of that happens without agencies willing to let people move past the boundaries of a brief. Rashi Garodia, Business Head at Team Pumpkin, believes it is a matter of trust. "Freedom in an agency today is not about removing boundaries; it is about giving people the confidence to push those boundaries," she says. "When you give people the room to make decisions, and the comfort to learn when things don't work, you don't just get better ideas, you build people who think and act like leaders."

Upasana Naithani, Head of Business at Punt Creative, says that confidence is now most visible among the youngest people in the room. "The work we finally ship looks nothing like what the brief originally asked for, but it solves the actual brand or business problem underneath," she comments. “It’s usually our youngest team members, and they’re given the space to push back not just internally but with a marketing head, sometimes a CMO, in the room. Creative freedom was always the licence to make something unexpected. The freedom that matters now is the safety to say ‘the brief is asking the wrong question’ — and be heard, regardless of how many years you’ve worked.”

Sreedharan similarly believes agencies need to give employees more freedom to challenge the status quo rather than simply execute what has already been decided. He argues that agencies can give teams a clear business challenge and guardrails, while allowing them to determine how the problem should be solved. This becomes particularly relevant with AI and emerging technologies, where smaller teams could be given the room to test whether a tool genuinely improves a client problem, workflow or idea.

"An agency does its best work when people are encouraged to challenge the obvious answer, question what the brief is really trying to solve and bring perspectives that the client may not have considered," Sreedharan says.

What the next generation is actually asking for

That question, what will the next generation of advertising professionals value most, gets answered differently once you move past hierarchy and into identity. 

Saumya Baijal, Executive Vice President, Strategy at Virtue Asia, India, reveals the coming generation wants permission to get things wrong in public. "We have put far too much pressure on getting to answers quickly," she says. But the generation that is coming understands the importance of errors- what they teach, how enriching the journey becomes, and how pressurised life becomes when forced to keep finding ways to live without them. They will seek the freedom to fail. The other will be the freedom to reinvent themselves. Choose a different path midway.”

Similarly, Mangtani believes the next generation will value the freedom to remain dynamic rather than being confined to the role they were hired for. She points to a growing desire among younger professionals to understand the "why" and the "what", rather than simply execute the "how". That could mean a creative wanting to present an idea, appear on camera or contribute to strategy, and more broadly, build a career that is not restricted by a job description.

"The next generation will value the freedom to be dynamic the most," Mangtani says.

Similarly, Sneha Desai, Design Lead at Wife, thinks of it as freedom from the pressure of certainty. 

"The freedom to make mistakes, experiment and explore the unknown, without feeling like every idea needs to have a guaranteed outcome," is what she believes the next wave of talent wants most.

Dipshika Ravi, National Creative Director at Schbang, takes a similar view, but places disagreement at the centre of that freedom. She believes the strongest work often emerges when people feel comfortable challenging an answer regardless of designation, something that requires trust and psychological safety. For the next generation, she says, freedom will mean being able to question assumptions, challenge the brief and have a genuine voice in shaping the work.

"For me, freedom today means the freedom to disagree. The best work I have been part of has come from rooms where someone felt comfortable saying, 'I don't think this is the right answer,' regardless of their designation," Ravi says.

Given what young talent is asking for, the practical question becomes where agencies can actually hand over ownership rather than just exposure. Naithani notes, "Let people own problems, not tasks... Real ownership is giving someone a whole client question end to end, including the freedom to get it wrong." 

Baijal wants agencies to build "thinking labs" internally, spaces built specifically for ideas that are allowed to keep failing until one works. 

Desai points to social media as the obvious training ground, "an evolving space without a fixed playbook," where junior teams can shape the rules rather than inherit them. And Daswani ties ownership back to confidence: give a young planner or designer a thought to carry "from observation to execution," she says, because that is "where confidence, judgement and, ultimately, better advertising are built."

Sangwan notes, “Agencies that empower employees to experiment with new formats, AI-driven workflows, strategic thinking, and cross-functional collaboration without the fear of failure will not only build stronger teams but also create more innovative work for their clients."

There is a version of this industry that needed less freedom, not more. The rules against misleading claims, against products dressed up as miracles, against ads that lied to sell, were restrictions worth having. They made advertising accountable to the people it spoke to. But David Ogilvy, one of the industry's founding voices, saw the other side of that coin. "Remove advertising, disable a person or firm from proclaiming its wares and their merits, and the whole of society and of the economy is transformed," he wrote. "The enemies of advertising are the enemies of freedom."

That tension, between the restraint advertising needs and the freedom it depends on, is not new. What has changed is who gets to hold both ideas at once. It used to be the domain of the CEO or the creative director. Now, if the people quoted here are right, it belongs to whoever is closest to the problem, regardless of their title or their years on the job.

item.title: Shonali Chakravarty joins United Breweries as Lead - Communications, Sustainability & CSR
item.description:
Shonali Chakravarty has been appointed Lead - Communications, Sustainability and CSR at United Breweries Limited (UBL) for its India business.

Chakravarty announced the move in a LinkedIn post, saying she was joining UBL, a HEINEKEN company, after six years at Lenovo, where she led enterprise communications across Asia Pacific.

“Some career moves are about going further. Some are about going deeper,” she wrote.

She said the move marks a shift from enterprise technology to the alcoholic beverages industry, adding, “It’s a very different industry from enterprise technology. And that is precisely what makes this move so exciting.”

Chakravarty said her previous roles at companies including Uber, OYO and Lenovo involved working across growth, technology, regulation, public policy and reputation.

“Over the years, I’ve had the opportunity to work across businesses that sit at the intersection of growth, technology, regulation, public policy and reputation. From Uber and OYO to Lenovo, each came with its own complexity, its own stakeholders and, occasionally, its own version of a five-alarm fire,” she wrote.

On her new role, she said the alcoholic beverages industry presents a different set of challenges because it is “deeply regulated, highly state-specific and shaped by an unusually broad stakeholder ecosystem.”

She added that her mandate at UBL goes beyond communications.

“And at UBL, the mandate goes well beyond communications. Bringing Communications, Sustainability and CSR together creates an opportunity to think about reputation and responsible business as one connected agenda. From how a company communicates to how it operates, creates impact and earns trust. That feels like the right kind of next chapter for me,” she wrote.

Chakravarty also reflected on changes in the communications profession and said leadership roles are increasingly being defined by their proximity to the business and the responsibility they carry beyond communications.

“The most interesting leadership opportunities today aren’t necessarily defined by a bigger geography or a bigger team. They are defined by how closely the mandate sits to the business and how much responsibility leaders are given for shaping the organization beyond its narrative,” she wrote.

She said the move from an APAC communications role at a technology company to a broader enterprise role covering communications, sustainability and CSR at a consumer business represents that shift.

Chakravarty has held communications and corporate affairs roles at Lenovo, OYO, Uber and Essar. At Lenovo, she led communications and analyst relations for its Infrastructure Solutions Group and later expanded her remit to cover the company’s Infrastructure Solutions Group and Solutions and Services Group across Asia Pacific.

At OYO, she served as Director of Corporate Communications, while at Uber she held communications roles covering policy and corporate communications for India and South Asia.

Her earlier experience includes leading strategic and digital communications for Essar Oil and Essar Power, as well as marketing and communications at Marsh. She began her communications career in public affairs at Edelman.

Chakravarty ended her announcement on a lighter note, writing, “And, of course, there’s something delightfully unexpected about going from deep tech to beer! Turns out, after years of talking about AI, cloud and the future of computing, I’m now thinking about another kind of cloud. The one above a perfectly poured pint.
